data.title: Is your job the right fit for you and top things to know about investing
data.description:
Synopsis: Every Monday, get a head start in your personal finance, career and life with hosts Sue-Ann Tan and See Kai Wen.

Ever wondered if you can find true friendship in the office?

We explore the boundaries of workplace friendships, discuss the risk of mixing work with personal relationships (even with your podcast co-host), and why office dynamics can often mirror toxic school cliques.

Can personality tests like the MBTI help determine the best job for you? Career coach and co-founder of Strengths School Jason Ho joins us to discuss why your interests may not always align with your natural skills.

We also talk about how to successfully strike a balance between passion and practical strengths in your professional life.

Are wedding proposals in Singapore not romantic anymore?

Kai Wen and guest host Isabelle discuss how shifting societal norms in Singapore have changed wedding proposals. Are elaborate gestures are still necessary? Or is it the underlying effort what truly counts?

ETFs, REITs, SSBs, T-bills - what do they all mean?

In this episode, we break down different investment assets to help you compare which ones are right for your portfolio with SGX director of capital market development Emelia Tan.

We also explore the rising popularity of ETFs, strategies for effective diversification, and the potential returns of the SGX versus the US stock market.

data.title: What to consider before investing in Anthropic
data.description:
Buying into Anthropic doesn’t feel like your typical single-stock bet. The artificial intelligence company lays out its great promise (curing diseases like cancer, developing drugs and other revolutionary innovations) and its most perilous downsides, among them “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

Placing a significant portion of your wealth on a single stock is never a good idea, but there’s always the temptation to buy something when a shiny new offering comes along. Research still shows that keeping a diversified mix of stocks and bonds over the long term is the best bet you can make.

data.title: MAS green-lights retail access to more complex funds; private market funds omitted for now
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Retail investors may soon be able to access a wider range of new fund product types as the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has implemented its revised Code on Collective Investment Schemes on Nov 26.

The amendments, which take effect immediately, follow a public consultation conducted between July 9 and Aug 10.

They delivered on a push first announced by Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong in June to help fund managers bring innovative products to market faster, amid growing investor sophistication and rising demand for a broader product shelf in Singapore.

Under the revised code, MAS introduced a Non-Traditional Funds Appendix to cater to new fund types that satisfy certain criteria.

Such funds are expected to involve non-traditional features, including the heavy use of derivatives. They would thus be classified as complex products under the complex products regime and enhanced distribution safeguards would apply accordingly, noted MAS.

The central bank said that it will work with market participants or relevant industry associations to develop requirements tailored to the features and risks of new fund types, which would be published in a circular.

This process is expected to take about three months upon receipt of all requisite information, down from six to 12 months previously.

Funds of the same type will take 21 days to be authorised if they meet the requirements, said MAS.

Market demand for specific fund types

MAS noted in July that it received market interest to offer two new fund types to retail investors: futures-based single-commodity funds and a wider range of single-country government bond funds.

During the recent public consultation, several respondents sought clarification on whether the proposed framework could accommodate other fund types, including those investing in private-market assets.

While the new appendix does not cover private-market investment funds, such as private equity or private credit, MAS clarified that such funds are being addressed under a separate retail framework to be released in due course.

As for futures-based single-commodity funds, the central bank said it must track a “well-recognised” futures prices index, for which it will consider the extent of its use as a benchmark by market participants and the length of its operational history.

There are five permitted commodities for this fund type: gold, silver, platinum, crude oil and iron ore.

Following industry feedback, MAS dropped its earlier proposal to bar the term “ETF” (exchange-traded fund) from these funds’ names, provided the name clearly specifies the commodity futures invested in.

However, prospectuses must detail the fund’s methodology for rolling futures contracts and illustrate how differences between futures prices across contract maturities can affect returns.

Separately, the central bank said it will proceed with recognising foreign funds that are comparable to new authorised fund products, including those under the new appendix.

To maintain a “level playing field”, MAS will establish safeguards in the Code on Collective Investment Schemes for an authorised fund before a comparable foreign fund type may be considered for recognition. THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Microdramas rake in US$20 billion as world gloms on to quick hits
data.description:
Minutes-long microdramas are set to notch US$20 billion (S$25.8 billion) in revenue in 2026 as global viewers swarm to their screens in search of quick, easy hits.

After the projected 24% growth globally in 2026, the market will expand further and rake in US$32 billion by 2031, according to a report by Media Partners Asia (MPA).

Audiences across the globe have latched on to the soapy serials, tailored to fit smartphones’ vertical screens and social-media scrollers’ fickle attention spans.

Cliffhangers, sudden tonal shifts and mafia-centred plot lines have fuelled the genre’s rise in popularity outside China, where they first took off, with major Hollywood players including Fox Entertainment, Walt Disney and Paramount+ beginning to explore the format.

Worldwide, one-tenth of people now watch the mini-films.

China still dominates most of the shows’ production and viewership.

TikTok parent ByteDance, Tencent Holdings and Kuaishou Technology pull in over 80% of the country’s US$15.2 billion in revenue from the films, MPA said.

In India, Asia’s second-largest market, local streamers like JioHotstar have drawn audiences with low-priced subscriptions billed outside app stores.

Yet, profit margins remain thin, particularly outside China.

More than half of revenue earned outside the country is burned on marketing to attract viewers who mostly watch for free, MPA said.

Producers are turning to artificial intelligence to pad their margins, though audiences have not taken to videos made with the technology.

About 75% of new titles on apps outside China in 2026 were generated with AI, but most top-viewed films on the platforms still feature live action, MPA estimates.

“AI has made a title cheap enough to test almost any idea, and catalogues have filled accordingly,” said Myat Pan Phyu, an analyst at MPA. “Viewing has moved far less.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: US leaves door open to lower Singapore tariff deal even as it proposes 20% levy
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The United States has left the door open to a trade deal that could lower tariffs on Singapore goods, even as it proposed a new levy of up to 20% on the Republic and 13 other trading partners.

United States Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate in a Nov 25 (Washington time) statement, which accused the 14 trading partners of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions.

“The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10% to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies and practices of Singapore,” the Office of the USTR said.

Without such a deal, the proposed tariff rate under Section 301 could reach up to 20% and take effect in early 2027.

However, the actual burden would be lower than 20%, as the rate will be net of previously announced Section 301 tariffs of 12.5% related to forced labour concerns. The proposal is also subject to a comment and hearing process through January, which could change the outcome.

“The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20%, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemptions for certain goods,” the USTR statement added.

The USTR said it will accept requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by Jan 5, 2027. Written comments are due by that same date. USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on Jan 25, 2027.

The US’ concerns are listed and explained at length in a separate 168-page USTR report that follows an investigation the agency started in March.

According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan, as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals industries.  

The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”.

Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) on Nov 26 expressed its disappointment over the new US tariffs, stating that the USTR’s probe leading to the proposed measure fails to take into account the unique structure of the Republic’s open, trade-reliant economy.

METI also said that Singapore “will continue to engage the USTR constructively, including to urge the USTR to reconsider its proposed actions on Singapore and to explore ways to reduce the tariff”.

However, it is still not clear if Singapore will negotiate an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the US.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at Singapore-based independent think-tank Hinrich Foundation, said the ART had not been on the table for either side until now because for Washington, Singapore was that rare country with which it had a trade surplus and an existing bilateral free trade agreement.

Now, however, “the US has certainly made clear their interest in negotiating an ART”, she said.

She said if the two sides enter talks, the US will likely demand three things: substantial new investments in the US; commitments to curb the flow of “non-market economy” (the US’ code for China) involvement in Singapore-to-US trade; and digital trade commitments that keep Singapore aligned with the US and American companies and platforms.

“Singapore will have to decide if these new commitments are worthwhile,” Elms added.

In its engagements with Trump administration officials since 2025, Singapore has persistently denied that it enjoys a trade surplus with the US or that its exports to the world’s largest economy stem from any form of excess capacity.

In fact, the US has maintained a substantial trade surplus with Singapore for more than two decades. In 2025, that surplus exceeded US$33 billion (S$42 billion), according to METI.

Singapore, despite its small size, is the third-largest Asian investor in the US, behind Japan and South Korea. Bilateral trade and Singapore investments in the US support some 350,000 American jobs.

About 6,600 US companies are based in Singapore, while more than 250 Singapore companies operate in 45 US states in sectors from logistics to agribusiness, to aerospace and shipbuilding.

However, the USTR report states: “Although Singapore has run a sizeable bilateral goods trade deficit with the United States for nearly all of the past decade, this does not outweigh the negative effects of Singapore’s outsized manufacturing sector and comparatively low consumption.

“If Singapore did not have acts, policies and practices contributing to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing, then the United States would be able to export more goods to Singapore beyond those it currently exports. 

“Moreover, Singapore’s trade surplus with key trading partners captures potential market share from US exporters in other markets.”

Adjusting these policies and initiatives to the liking of the US will be as hard as, if not more difficult than, dealing with earlier US tariffs related to the alleged trade of goods associated with forced labour.

In September, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said in the context of those earlier tariffs that Singapore will continue to engage the US on lowering tariffs and help businesses and workers adapt, but will consider any steps carefully in response to the negotiations.

As a major trading hub with around $2.5 trillion in goods and services trade each year, including $1.4 trillion in goods, any US import restrictions would have significant implications for Singapore’s trade, Gan had said on Sept 8.

Tommy Koh, a Singaporean former diplomat and the chief negotiator for the US-Singapore free trade agreement (FTA) inked in 2003, remarked on the irony of the situation: “The US is giving Singapore a Thanksgiving present.”

In a social media post on Nov 26, he said there was no justification for the proposal because of the FTA between the two countries. “The US cannot impose tariffs on Singapore. It will be a violation of the agreement,” he said.

He added that the US also has a trade surplus with Singapore in services, and pointed out a Heritage Foundation study that found the Republic to be the most free economy in the world.

“We export to the world in sectors where we have a comparative advantage, and we import in sectors where we don’t. This is called international trade,” Koh said.

“I would like to remind my American friends that the US is the second-largest exporter in the world. The US exports energy, aerospace products, pharmaceutical products, electronics and agricultural products. Using its own criterion, can we say the US has a structural excess industrial capacity in these sectors?” he added.

The USTR investigation into structural excess industrial capacity that is flooding world markets with cheap exports was conducted against a total of 16 trading partners, including close allies Japan, the European Union and South Korea.

The USTR has not proposed tariffs on goods from Mexico and Norway at the moment.

Affected trading partners besides Singapore are China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Some Singapore exports are also subject to US sectoral tariffs – with rates ranging from 25% to 50% – on steel, aluminium, copper and automotive parts.

data.title: CPF suppresses consumption? DPM Gan refutes US’ grounds for imposing higher tariffs
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 26 refuted the United States’ claim that the Central Provident Fund (CPF) scheme depresses Singaporeans’ consumption of goods – one of America’s allegations cited as the basis for new tariffs on the Republic.

In justifying its fresh levies of up to 20%, the Office of the US Trade Representative said that the Republic engaged in “savings promotion that depresses consumption and boosts Singapore’s current account surplus”.

The CPF scheme, in particular, mandated wage contributions “far beyond those of the United States and many developed economies”, it wrote in its 168-page report on Nov 25.

It argued that this, alongside other policies such as support for manufacturing and research and development, enhanced Singapore’s growth in capacity without commensurate growth in demand, to the detriment of US producers.

Speaking at a media briefing at The Treasury, Gan said Singapore has schemes that encourage, promote and support local consumption, citing CDC vouchers as an example.

He said CPF is not a scheme to suppress consumption but is aimed at meeting individuals’ housing, healthcare and retirement needs.

The system is critical to Singapore, given its ageing population, lack of natural resources and desire not to over-burden the younger generation.

It is also unique to Singapore, he noted. “Most countries, either they have a pension fund or they have an insurance scheme that they rely on for their retirement needs.”

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that Singapore would continue to engage the US and work towards a reduction of tariffs on local companies.

“So I think it will be important for us to communicate with them to explain our position to them, and we hope that they will understand what CPF is about.”

data.title: Keppel weighs sale of StarHub stake after M1 deal, says telco was ‘only realistic partner’
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Keppel, which owns M1, is considering three options to monetise the 23% stake in the enlarged StarHub it would receive if the proposed merger between the two telcos goes through.

It could sell the shares over time, sell them to a strategic investor or fund, or distribute them directly to its shareholders, Keppel chief executive Loh Chin Hua said on Nov 26, responding to investor queries in a filing with the Singapore Exchange. A combination of the three options could also be taken.

Loh said the merger with StarHub is step one of a “two-stage divestment” as part of the company’s strategy to become more asset-light and monetise its non-core assets by 2030.

The deal would take about $324 million in M1 net debt off Keppel’s books and free it from having to fund the telco’s capital expenditure, including investments in its technology infrastructure, cyber resilience, network and spectrum.

“If we continue to own M1 as a subsidiary, we would... also continue to consolidate its results, including losses such as those we saw in the first half of 2026,” Loh said. M1 recorded a net loss of $9.2 million for the first six months of the year.

Concerns have been raised about Keppel’s agreement to the all-share deal proposed by StarHub, as it is worth less than Australia-backed telco Simba’s $1.4 billion all-cash deal for its failed merger with M1.

The $65 million loss from the failed merger in May contributed to the group’s $375 million net losses in its non-core portfolio for the first half of its 2026 financial year, which dragged net profit down by 59%.

Loh said StarHub was the “only realistic merger partner”, and an all-share deal “makes sense for both sides”. While the enlarged telco is able to conserve cash for integration and growth, Keppel would also be able to reap the benefits of market consolidation.

He noted that M1 contributed $3 million to Keppel’s profit in FY2025.

In contrast, even a 10-cent rise in StarHub’s share price over a year would add about $55 million to the value of Keppel’s stake, he added. Should the telco continue to pay six cents per share for its ordinary dividends, Keppel would be entitled to receive an additional $33 million in cash.

Altogether, this would result in about $88 million in value appreciation and dividends for the year.

Keppel stands to gain about $268 million if its 546.5 million StarHub shares rise from its pre-announcement price of $1.01 to $1.50 according to projections, as a result of cost savings and greater growth resulting from market consolidation.

This is “significant”, Loh said, adding: “Thus, we believe that the benefits of deconsolidating M1 and the longer-term potential of our stake in the combined entity make this a very good trade for Keppel.”

Analysts told The Straits Times that Keppel is likely to benefit more from remaining invested in the enlarged StarHub group rather than exiting immediately with cash.

The newly announced merger, which also comes just six months after Simba’s bid collapsed, is also timely, with Keppel still aiming to divest a total of $13.7 billion in non-core assets by 2030.

OCBC equity research analyst Chu Peng said that while Keppel would not be able to issue a special dividend yet from the M1 sale, the 12-month lock-up period allows it to retain exposure to the estimated $1.1 billion in cost savings as well as potential revenue growth and any subsequent re-rating.

“Keppel still intends to monetise the stake by 2030, but we believe it would first want the enlarged StarHub to deliver on the expected synergies and potentially re-rate before exiting.”

On the flip side, Keppel could also be exposed to volatility in StarHub’s share price and potentially a wider conglomerate discount until a clearer exit path is apparent, noted CGS International’s analysts Lim Siew Khee and Meghana Kande.

Keppel can only exercise its options to monetise its StarHub stake as early as the first half of 2028, they noted.

The analysts cut their target price for Keppel from $13.52 to $11.22, but maintained their “Add” rating, noting that the group remains focused on being a global asset manager.

“Keppel’s focus is to build a global franchise as an infrastructure asset manager and operator, and it has a wide network of investors or limited partners it can tap to divest,” noted Paul Chew, head of research at Phillip Securities Research.

In the meantime, with the integration of M1 in StarHub’s business likely to be a complex, costly and time-consuming process, Keppel’s board seat on the telco will be useful to support the merger, he said.

He added that following Keppel’s divestment of M1, its next priority would be to complete construction and delivery of four offshore rigs which it would charter out to Seatrium for an eventual sale.

Other non-core assets that Keppel would be looking to offload include real estate, investment properties and its land bank, with the timing dependent on market conditions and achievable valuations, said OCBC’s Chu.

Keppel’s shares fell from $8.87 after the merger was announced on Nov 24 to a low of $8.30 before rebounding. They closed 0.84% higher at $8.39 on Nov 26.

The company’s share price has been under pressure since the start of the year due to a combination of factors, including weaker-than-expected headline earnings from losses in its non-core legacy businesses, Chu pointed out.

“The all-share StarHub-M1 transaction could also disappoint investors hoping for more immediate value realisation, with monetisation of Keppel’s stake likely to take time.”

Continued earnings growth and execution of its asset-light strategy should help reinforce confidence in Keppel’s transformation and support a recovery in its share price, she said.

Meanwhile, StarHub’s shares continued to climb after it announced its merger with M1, closing 1.8% higher at $1.11 on Nov 26.

data.title: South Korea hikes interest rates again to 3.25% as AI boom powers growth and inflation
data.description:
The Bank of Korea (BOK) resumed raising interest rates while sharply increasing its growth forecast for 2027, in a sign that the tightening cycle may last longer than previously expected as a historic semiconductor boom powers the economy.

The central bank increased its seven-day repurchase rate by a quarter percentage point to 3.25% in a 5-2 decision on Nov 26, a move predicted by 21 of 23 economists surveyed by Bloomberg.

The hike follows a pause in October after back-to-back increases in July and August, bringing the tightening in 2026 to 75 basis points.

South Korea’s export-driven economy has been powered by an exceptionally strong memory-chip cycle tied to the global artificial intelligence build-out. Alongside the rate decision, the BOK raised its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 3.9% and 4.1%, respectively, up from 3.3% for 2026 and 2.9% for 2027 in August.

“By acting pre-emptively, we can limit the degree of tightening needed later and reap the benefits of acting early,” BOK governor Shin Hyun-song said after the board meeting. “We expect consumer-price inflation to converge to our target only in 2028.”

The Nov 26 move underscores the central bank’s focus on containing inflation as the semiconductor boom pushes growth beyond expectations. By resuming tightening after a one-meeting pause, policymakers are signalling that inflation and the strength of the export-driven expansion outweigh concerns about sluggish consumer spending and the recent stock market rout, at least for now.

“Next year’s growth forecast has topped 4%, which I attribute largely to the semiconductor sector’s rapidly expanding weight in the economy,” said Kong Dong-rak, a fixed-income strategist at Daishin Securities.

“By that measure, the 2027 outlook suggests the current tightening cycle could last longer and reach a higher peak than previously expected.”

The board’s updated six-month rate projections showed a median of 3.5%, up from 3.25% in August, pointing to scope for another rate hike. The outlook, covering December 2026 to May 2027, shows how policymakers are balancing persistent inflation against an uneven recovery.

The nation’s policy-sensitive three-year yield was up 4 basis points on the day at 3.63%, after rising as much as 6 basis points earlier as the central bank’s dot plot indicated the possibility of further policy tightening. The won remained largely unchanged at 1,343.35 per US dollar.

Governor Shin has repeatedly said the bank will maintain a restrictive policy until it is confident inflation is converging towards its 2% target.

He has likened the BOK’s approach to using a “homi”, a small Korean hand plough, rather than a larger “garae” or shovel, describing the earlier back-to-back hikes as pre-emptive moves to keep inflation from becoming entrenched.

The BOK raised its 2027 inflation forecast to 2.4% from 2.3%, reflecting expectations that price pressures will remain elevated as stronger economic growth feeds into domestic demand. It kept its consumer price index forecast for 2026 unchanged at 2.7%.

Consumer prices rose 2.8% in October from a year earlier, slowing from 2.9% in September while core inflation, excluding food and energy, edged up to 2.8%, leaving both measures above the BOK’s 2% target.

Kwon Hyo-sung, economist at Bloomberg Economics, said: “The stock market rout didn’t stop the Bank of Korea from raising its policy rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, as we expected.

“With inflation still stubbornly above target, strong growth gave the board room to act. We expect another hike to 3.5% in February 2027, though a slowdown in global AI-related investment would put that call at risk.”

South Korea’s economy expanded 1% in the third quarter from the previous three months, exceeding economists’ expectations for a 0.8% gain as exports and investment surged. Still, private consumption contracted unexpectedly, underscoring how little of the chip-driven boom has filtered through to households.

The export boom has shown little sign of losing momentum since then. In October, shipments adjusted for working-day differences jumped about 76% from a year earlier, with semiconductors continuing to drive the gains.

South Korea last week also surpassed US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion) in cumulative goods exports for the first time, becoming only the fourth country to reach the milestone in a calendar year. 

Shin argued that the benefits of the chip boom will eventually spread through the broader economy, even if the transmission to household consumption remains weak for now.

He estimated semiconductor companies’ operating profits at nearly 700 trillion won (S$672.2 billion) in 2026, more than a fifth of national income, with an unusually large share of income accruing to corporate profits rather than wages. Those earnings will ultimately filter through the economy via corporate taxes, bonuses, dividends and investment, he said, though the process may take time. BLOOMBERG

data.title: OCBC expands physical gold business with new 100-tonne vault in Singapore
data.description:
SINGAPORE – OCBC has added a 100-tonne dedicated gold vault in Singapore, expanding its physical gold business to meet increasing appetite for trading and custody services.

The new facility – capable of holding some 8,000 large gold bars weighing 12.4kg each – complements the bank’s existing vaulting arrangements in the Republic, OCBC said on Nov 26.

It serves OCBC’s institutional clients as well as those of its private banking subsidiary, Bank of Singapore.

OCBC declined to disclose how much physical gold it currently holds in custody and the number of clients it stores gold for, but noted that it has seen growing demand for its services, especially from Bank of Singapore clients seeking secure, long-term custody arrangements.

OCBC said it is “seeing increasing interest in its custody and vaulting services among its institutional clients, particularly banks and private banks”.

Kenneth Lai, head of global markets at OCBC, said interest in physical gold has been strong since the bank launched its physical gold business in June.

This, he said, reflects “growing demand from clients seeking secure and Singapore-based solutions in relation to their physical gold needs”.

The new vault comes as the Republic steps up efforts to strengthen its position as a leading gold trading and distribution hub in the Asia-Pacific region.

OCBC is a founding clearing member of an over-the-counter gold clearing system which the Singapore Exchange is set to launch in 2027.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) on Nov 10 launched a gold vaulting service for foreign central banks, international financial institutions and sovereign entities looking to hold their gold reserves in Singapore.

The gold will be stored in MAS’ national currency vault, which can hold up to 500 tonnes of the precious metal, with room to expand as demand grows.

The service will complement Singapore’s commercial vaulting capacity of more than 2,000 tonnes, which serves market participants such as bullion banks, institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals.

MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to selected Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to foreign central banks, international financial institutions and sovereign entities.

OCBC said it will continue to explore extending its offerings in physical gold, as well as other physical gold-linked investment and hedging solutions, to more client segments across the group.

Its asset management arm, Lion Global Investors, launched the LionGlobal Singapore Physical Gold Fund in 2025, Singapore’s first fund backed by physical gold that is insured and stored in the Republic.

This was followed by the listing of the LionGlobal Singapore Physical Gold exchange-traded fund (ETF), Singapore’s first home-grown physical gold ETF, on SGX in March 2026.

Retail clients in Singapore can also invest in fractional gold or silver through the OCBC app, while clients of its insurance arm Great Eastern can gain exposure to physical gold through investment-linked policies.

data.title: New Air India chief seeks to cut $837 million in costs
data.description:
Air India is looking to cut costs by 60 billion rupees (S$837 million) this financial year as its new chief executive outlined initiatives to revive the loss-making airline, sources familiar with the matter said. 

Key steps announced at a town hall meeting with CEO Tewolde Gebremariam on Nov 25 include the merger of some departments at Air India and its budget unit, starting a dedicated cargo service and introducing holiday packages, said the sources, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. 

Westbound flights, which generally head to the Middle East and Europe, will be shifted from New Delhi to Mumbai and Bengaluru, the sources said.

That should help shorten detours needed to avoid Pakistan’s airspace, which has been closed to Indian carriers since April 2025, when relations between the neighbours deteriorated following a deadly attack in Kashmir.

Tewolde, the former CEO of Ethiopian Airlines Group, joined Air India in September with the task of turning around the struggling carrier.

He has sought to reduce maintenance costs and is considering folding budget carrier Air India Express into the main group. 

Air India lost more than 220 billion rupees in the last financial year following a series of challenges including a deadly crash in June 2025, the closure of Pakistani airspace and the war in Iran which disrupted flights and drove up fuel expenses.

The weaker Indian rupee has also added to its financial woes, since much of the airline’s costs are in US dollars.

Air India did not respond to requests to confirm Tewolde’s comments at the town hall meeting.

He also raised the issue of efficiency at the meeting, and asked workers to show more urgency in turning around flights, the people said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: ASEAN must counter economic nationalism with deeper integration, wider partnerships: DPM Gan
data.description:
SINGAPORE – ASEAN must counter rising economic nationalism with deeper integration and wider partnerships, in a world where governments are placing more emphasis on self-reliance and control over critical industries, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 27.

“Raising barriers among ourselves would narrow the opportunities available to each of us,” he said. A more integrated ASEAN would strengthen its value as a partner, while broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his speech, Gan identified three factors that make integration and partnerships especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks and geo-economic contestation. “Each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward. Yet each also makes cooperation more crucial,” he said.

His remarks followed the United States’ announcements of fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves which affected many in South-east Asia as the region finds itself in the crosshairs of sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“Geo-economic competition is reshaping the networks through which we trade, invest and access technology,” Gan said, with governments paying closer attention to dependencies and control over critical capabilities.

“ASEAN countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences,” he added. “But we can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment and cooperation.”

Doing so would require that ASEAN earn and sustain its partners’ confidence in the grouping’s integrity, institutional reliability and business environment by issuing clear and predictable rules, upholding its laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing, he said.

“As scrutiny of international trade and investment intensifies, maintaining these standards becomes even more important,” he added.

ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027, with Singapore pushing for deeper integration and wider partnerships as it takes on ASEAN’s rotating chairmanship at a time of heightened geopolitical contestation.

Both the US and China would continue to be key economic partners for ASEAN, Gan said, with their businesses, technologies and markets important to the region’s growth.

Both countries are among the region’s largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

In tandem, the grouping is strengthening tie-ups with other partners that would expand the region’s economic options and reduce its exposure to disruptions, Gan said.

These include negotiations to upgrade ASEAN’s trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand and enhance the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with other regional groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

ASEAN is also strengthening integration within the grouping, with Gan highlighting recent efforts that would help firms better tap suppliers and customers within the region.

A recently upgraded ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement, set to be rolled out in end-2026, will help businesses reduce costs through streamlined procedures and more transparent rules, he said, while a customs-related mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances and priority treatment in participating countries.

And a regional Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month would make cross-border transactions, payments and access to digital services easier, he added.

These would make ASEAN more valuable as a place to produce and market to serve, and form a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to “engage the world with greater confidence”, Gan said.

data.title: 2 companies linked to lash, hair and nails chain Milly’s wound up after outlets closed
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Two companies associated with Milly’s, a well-known Singapore salon chain offering beauty services such as lash and hair extensions, have been wound up.

Milly’s Group and its wholly owned subsidiary, Milly’s Co. Singapore, were wound up by High Court orders on Nov 13, according to notices published in the Government Gazette on Nov 20, which said creditors should submit their proofs of debt to liquidators.

Maybank Singapore was the claimant in both cases. It filed the winding-up application on Oct 21.

Gary Loh and Dev Kumar Harish Nandwani of BDO Advisory were appointed liquidators of both companies.

In response to The Straits Times’ queries, the liquidators said the company’s outlets had ceased operations before the winding-up order. They are taking control of assets and records, and will assess creditors’ claims, they said.

The liquidators also said they were reviewing the company’s records to determine customers’ unused prepaid packages. Customers with packages that have not been fully used may submit a proof of debt with supporting documents, they added.

Checks were also being conducted to see if sums remained owing to former employees. Those with outstanding salary or other entitlements may submit claims to the liquidators, they said.

Milly’s website continued to list a phone number and an email address for customers to contact for package enquiries, verification and appointment arrangements on Nov 25, but the site is now offline.

Go-to for eyelash and hair extensions

Milly’s first opened at Far East Plaza in 2008. It became a go-to spot for eyelash and hair extensions at a time when such services were less widely available here, and expanded to other mall outlets over the years.

Milly’s Group was incorporated in 2011, and the subsidiary Milly’s Co. Singapore, formerly known as Milly’s (Orchard), in 2015. Emily Xu was listed as a director of both companies.

Online listings now show Milly’s outlets at Plaza Singapura, JEM, Tanjong Pagar, Tampines 1 and Suntec City marked as permanently closed. It is not known when the original Milly’s outlet at Far East Plaza exited the mall.

ST checks found that Milly’s Facebook account has been deactivated, while its Instagram account has been rebranded as Mii Wellness. Incorporated in June, Mii has a different shareholder and director.

Mii Wellness’ social media profile lists locations at Tanjong Pagar Plaza and JEM, which were previously Milly’s outlets, and Tampines Downtown Line station.

ST has contacted Milly’s and the Ministry of Manpower for further information.

data.title: Investment-linked insurance v participating plans: What drives demand and which suits you better
data.description:
SINGAPORE – After spending nearly a decade selling investment-linked insurance policies (ILPs) – hybrid products that combine investing with insurance coverage – former financial adviser Bobby Sim said the experience was “one of the reasons I could not stay in the industry”.

Sim, who worked at Manulife and later at advisory firm Finexis, shared that high commissions, particularly in the first two years of a policy, heavily incentivise insurance agents to push ILPs.

“Most of us sold what the company recommended, without fully understanding the returns behind the product,” he said.

“I am not saying every agent is bad. But if you look at net returns after fees, most of the ILPs I saw did worse than simply putting the money into the S&P 500.”

That experience shaped his personal financial planning – he now keeps his investments separate from his family’s insurance protection needs. 

“When you mix the two in one product, you usually get a worse version of both,” he noted.

That said, Sim feels that ILPs may still suit three types of buyers: those who lack the discipline to save; those whose advisers can help them achieve market-beating returns after fees; and those who lack the bandwidth to manage their own finances and prefer leaving both insurance and investments to a trusted adviser.

Buyers are still signing up

Latest figures from the Life Insurance Association Singapore (LIA) show that sales of new ILPs – measured by weighted new business premiums – rose 22.6% year on year to $2.51 billion in the first nine months of 2026.

These plans made up 46% of all new sales, up from 43% over the same period in 2025 and 37% in 2024.

Participating (par) life insurance policies also recorded growth, with weighted new sales rising 5.7% to $1.24 billion over the same nine-month period.

Par plans accounted for 23% of all new sales in the first nine months of 2026, down slightly from 25% in the corresponding periods of 2024 and 2025.  

These plans fall into three categories: whole life insurance, endowment savings plans and retirement income plans.

Rachel Luo, senior director of sales at Manulife Advisory Group, said interest in ILPs and par plans is driven by greater awareness of long-term financial planning, concerns about the rising cost of living and the financial implications of longer lifespans, as well as a desire for structure and discipline.

Many consumers lack the time, knowledge and confidence to manage a portfolio actively, she added. 

While both types of policies have investment components, they work differently, and the choice between an ILP and a par plan ultimately comes down to how much risk a consumer can bear.

ILPs versus par plans 

Helen Shen, group head of products at Singlife, said ILPs bundle insurance protection with market exposure through investment sub-funds. 

A policy’s value depends on the performance of the funds, minus insurance charges and other fees.

Returns fluctuate with the market, and policyholders bear all the investment risk.

These products therefore suit customers who are comfortable riding out market cycles for potentially higher returns and want more flexibility in choosing their own funds, Shen noted. 

Manulife’s Luo sees interest in ILPs among younger and mid-career working adults, noting that these clients have longer investment horizons and are just starting to build their wealth and protection portfolios.

Unlike ILPs, which have no guaranteed cash value, par plans have a portion that is guaranteed.

Policyholders pay premiums that go into the insurer’s participating fund. They share in the fund’s profits and receive a combination of guaranteed benefits and non-guaranteed bonuses.

The guaranteed portion – known as the guaranteed surrender value – is smaller if they cash out early, while the full guaranteed benefit is paid if they hold to maturity.

In exchange for that stability, policyholders have no say in asset selection – the insurer decides how the money is invested across a portfolio of assets.

Shen noted that the “sweet spot” for par plans lies in balancing guaranteed benefits with non-guaranteed bonuses to boost total returns.

She added that this balance suits customers who are cautious about market volatility and want stability without giving up growth potential.

These customers are typically more focused on protecting and managing their wealth over the longer term, she said.

Luo pointed out that young families may buy whole life par plans to safeguard against the loss of a breadwinner’s income due to death, total and permanent disability, or critical illness.

Separately, endowment par policies are commonly used to fund children’s future education.  

Meanwhile, mid-career clients may use retirement income par plans for retirement planning, while individuals with more established financial portfolios may use whole life par policies for legacy planning, such as leaving a guaranteed inheritance for their children, Luo noted.

No financial plan is static. Shen noted that as customers move through different life stages and their financial needs evolve, they may require a mix of solutions to balance growth, protection and certainty.

“These approaches are not mutually exclusive,” she added.

“Ultimately, the choice between ILPs and par plans depends on an individual’s financial goals, investment horizon and risk appetite.”

A convenient bundle

For Manulife policyholder Anthony Lo, an ILP was “an educational experience”.

Lo appreciated having insurance coverage and investment options bundled in one plan, and the flexibility to decide how he wanted to invest his money. 

He stressed that buyers must look beyond the investment component and consider the insurance coverage, fees and charges.

“My personal experience is that ILPs are generally more suited to longer-term financial goals rather than short-term savings needs,” he said.

He also noted that returns are not guaranteed, and policy values can rise or fall with the markets.

A costly trap

While that two-in-one convenience worked for Lo, those very fees and lock-in charges turned an ILP into a costly trap for former agent Ang Jian Hui.

A relative convinced him to buy an ILP when he was younger.

However, after reviewing the policy and understanding its terms, he wanted to withdraw but could not because “I had to pay so much and forfeit my investment due to the lock-in charges”.

Ang shared that he had to wait eight years to break even.

“I felt like I wasted eight years,” he added.

When he was an agent, Ang avoided selling ILPs, opting instead to recommend endowment plans for clients who lack the discipline to save, and term plans for insurance protection needs.

For him, ILPs are expensive all-in-one products in which high investment fees and insurance charges could erode returns.

Know what you are buying 

Regardless of which option they choose, the onus falls on buyers to understand what they are signing up for.

“Before you invest in any financial product, invest in your own knowledge first,” said Sim, who now runs his own durian business.

“Nobody cares about your money more than you do.”

data.title: Singapore factory output up 6.1% in October as AI demand remains robust
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore’s manufacturing output expanded in October, on the back of sustained demand for AI- and semiconductor-related products that supported the electronics and precision engineering sectors.

Factory output grew 6.1% year on year, up from September’s revised pace of 5%, according to data released by the Economic Development Board (EDB) on Nov 26. All clusters posted gains except transport engineering and biomedical manufacturing.

The figure exceeded the 2.2% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll. Excluding the highly volatile biomedical manufacturing sector, output increased 12.1%.

Analysts say Singapore’s manufacturing growth accelerated despite high base effects, and the outlook remains constructive for the near term. But industries outside the AI and tech spheres could see muted growth in the fourth quarter.

DBS Bank senior economist Chua Han Teng said the global AI-driven expansion “still has legs”, though it is likely to proceed at a more sustainable pace, resulting in respectable albeit moderate growth in Singapore’s manufacturing sector.

Downside risks to the global AI cycle could include tighter financial conditions and US-led regulatory measures, amid closer investor scrutiny of returns on AI investment.

UOB economist Jester Koh said these could moderate AI-related tailwinds in the second half of 2027, as hyperscalers are also expected to slow down their capital expenditure growth.

Newly proposed US tariffs of up to 20% could hit the Republic’s non-oil domestic exports and thus the manufacturing sector.

Chua said Singapore still has room until January 2027 to negotiate with the US, reflecting ongoing active bilateral engagements and goodwill.

In the meantime, continued exemptions for semiconductor and pharmaceutical goods would help keep the downside impact on Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports to the US manageable.

The precision engineering cluster grew the most, at 54.1%, driven by higher production of semiconductor equipment in the machinery and systems segment, which surged 62.4%. Precision modules and components saw production increase by 16.1%.

Maybank economist Brian Lee said that the rise in demand for semiconductor equipment could be partially attributed to expansions at local and regional chip fabrication plants.

Output from the electronics cluster continued to expand year on year due to continued AI demand, with 6.6% growth. Other electronic modules and components saw the largest output, climbing 26.9%, followed by the computer peripherals and data storage segment, growing 24.7%.

Production in the semiconductors segment grew 5.2%, while the infocommunications and consumer electronics segment gained 5.3%.

Strong AI infrastructure build-out led by US hyperscalers will continue to fuel demand for AI-related products, with electronics and precision engineering firms staying optimistic for the October 2026 to March 2027 period, said Chua.

The chemicals cluster grew 4.4%, after contracting in September.

The expansion was led by a 10.4% uptick in the specialities segment due to higher production of industrial gases, chemicals and food additives, as well as a 16.6% increase in the other chemicals segment thanks to higher output of fragrances.

The petroleum segment grew 7.8% on higher production of refined products. The petrochemicals segment continued to shrink, declining 23.1% amid softer demand and feedstock supply disruptions that constrained production.

UOB’s Koh said the strength in the petroleum segment reflected a recovery in supplies from the Middle East. This was likely aided by bypass pipelines and alternative ports, increased Gulf production and continued transit through the Strait of Hormuz via shuttle tankers.

General manufacturing industries grew 0.5%, with the food, beverages and tobacco segment climbing 2.1% on higher production of milk powder and beverage products.

The miscellaneous and printing segments, however, recorded output dips of 1.3% and 10.2%, respectively, with miscellaneous weighed down by lower production of structural metal products and furniture.

The transport engineering cluster declined 5.3% due to lower shipyard activities and weak production of oil and gas field equipment in the marine and offshore engineering segment, which contracted 25.2%.

The land transport segment expanded the most, at 34.3%, while the aerospace segment edged up 0.8%, supported by higher production of aircraft parts and engine maintenance, repair and overhaul.

The biomedical manufacturing segment declined 35.8% due to lower production of biologics and a change in the mix of active pharmaceutical ingredients in the pharmaceuticals segment.

data.title: Singapore ‘very disappointed’ by proposed US tariffs, says move overlooks its economic structure
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore has expressed disappointment over proposed US tariffs, stating that the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) probe has failed to consider the unique structure of the Republic’s open, trade-reliant economy.

“Singapore disagrees with the USTR’s findings and we are very disappointed with the proposed actions against Singapore,” said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) in a Nov 26 statement.

The response comes after the USTR proposed on Nov 25 to impose tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore and 13 other trading partners under Section 301, accusing them of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions.

The duties could take effect in early 2027, though USTR Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington.

METI said Singapore “will continue to engage the USTR constructively, including to urge the USTR to reconsider its proposed actions on Singapore and to explore ways to reduce the tariff”.

The USTR also issued a 168-page investigation report listing and explaining US concerns that follow the investigation the agency started in March.

According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan; as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health and petrochemicals industries.

The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”.

METI said: “The USTR’s findings do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.

“Singapore’s global trade surplus is a reflection of our outward- and market-oriented economy, as well as our status as a trusted business and trading hub.”

As a small country with limited resources, Singapore’s priority is to ensure that markets operate efficiently, and that the economy remains competitive globally, it said.

“Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidise manufacturing for export. Our free trade agreements seek to lower barriers to trade and investments, and are fully compliant with World Trade Organization rules,” it added.

METI said the US-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (USSFTA) is an example of how trade with the Republic has worked for the US.

Under the USSFTA, Singapore levies no tariffs on US exports to Singapore, and the US has committed to levying no tariffs on imports from Singapore.

Since the USSFTA was signed, the US has enjoyed a consistent trade surplus with Singapore for more than 20 years.

In 2024, the US’ overall trade surplus with the Republic amounted to US$27 billion (S$34.8 billion). In 2025, this trade surplus with Singapore grew to US$33 billion.

However, the USTR report states: “Although Singapore has run a sizeable bilateral goods trade deficit with the United States for nearly all of the past decade, this does not outweigh the negative effects of Singapore’s outsized manufacturing sector and comparatively low consumption.”

METI said the ministry engaged the agency actively throughout the USTR investigation, and thoroughly addressed its queries and concerns.

It added that it will submit further comments during the upcoming public consultation period in January to address the issues raised in the report.

data.title: Panadol maker Haleon launches innovation hub in Singapore, to invest $100m annually in regional R&D
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Panadol maker Haleon launched a healthcare innovation hub in Singapore on Nov 25, which will tap the city-state’s research capabilities and startup ecosystem to develop products tailored to the needs of Asian consumers.

The new Future of Health Innovation Hub, supported by Singapore’s Economic Development Board, will see Haleon invest more than $100 million in research and innovation across the Asia-Pacific (APAC) annually.

The British firm, best known for consumer healthcare brands Panadol, Advil and Sensodyne, was spun off from the consumer health division of pharmaceutical giant GSK in 2022. Haleon is listed in London and New York.

The hub will focus its R&D efforts particularly in Haleon’s oral health brands such as Sensodyne, and wellness brands including Centrum and Caltrate.

Its research and innovation efforts will utilise consumer insights, scientific expertise, digital capabilities and artificial intelligence-enabled technologies to develop science-backed products for APAC consumers.

Haleon will also pursue innovation through partnerships with academic institutions and government agencies, including specialised research institutes at the National University of Singapore, Nanyang Technological University and A*Star.

The company also said it will work with local startup partners such as microbiome company Amili and cognitive health technology provider Gray Matter Solutions.

These partnerships are intended to drive clinical studies and academic research relevant to Asian populations, to develop innovations focused on healthy ageing, health inclusivity and condition awareness.

Ho Weng Si, executive vice-president at the Economic Development Board, said Haleon’s decision to launch the innovation hub in Singapore reflects the strength of the city-state’s innovation ecosystem, while enabling the company to develop its consumer health solutions for the wider region.

Singapore also serves as the company’s headquarters for APAC, where Haleon operates across 18 markets.

Keith Choy, Asia-Pacific president at Haleon, noted that the company’s efforts in APAC will contribute significantly to its global ambition to reach one billion new consumers by 2030.

He said that the region’s varying levels of economic development and diverse demographic profiles present different opportunities for the consumer healthcare industry – from ageing populations to younger, more health-conscious consumers.

In the Philippines, for instance, Haleon has introduced single-unit packaging for its Centrum nutritional supplements to make them more affordable to lower-income consumers.

“Asia’s diversity is its biggest opportunity,” he said, adding that APAC is the most populous region served by Haleon.

Speaking at the launch, Singapore Senior Minister of State for Health Tan Kiat How noted that Haleon’s innovation hub aligns with the city-state’s efforts to enhance the health of its residents amid increasingly longer lifespans.

Tan, who is also senior minister of state for digital development and information, said Singapore is increasingly moving its healthcare priorities upstream, from treating illnesses to preventing them.

“(The innovation hub) can explore ways to make preventive health more personal, accessible and actionable,” he said.

Tan noted that Singapore has a strong research and healthcare ecosystem, with a track record of bringing researchers and the public and private sectors together to drive innovation.

“It is about combining different strengths to turn promising ideas into practical solutions – developed with Asia’s needs in mind, and with the potential to benefit people not just in Singapore, not just in South-east Asia, but beyond.”

He added: “Ultimately, the measure of success is not how many new technologies we develop, but how many people can live healthier, more independent lives because of them.” THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Indonesia plans fee of 0.5% of export value of palm oil, association says
data.description:
JAKARTA – A firm set up by Indonesia to monitor commodity exports has proposed a charge of 0.5% of the export sales value of palm oil, an official of Indonesia’s palm oil association GAPKI said on Nov 26.

Palm oil exporters and industry groups were told of the fee during a briefing with Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI) on Nov 25, said Yustinus Lambang Setyo Putro, an association official.

DSI plans to collect a fixed fee of 2.5 million rupiah (S$176.52) for every contract palm oil exporters upload to its system and a verification fee of 0.5% of export sales value, Yustinus told Reuters.

A DSI spokesperson declined immediate comment on the plan.

“This is a burden,” said Mansuetus Darto, chairman of the smallholder palm oil farmers’ union POPSI. “Just for the sake of transparency by giving the exports data to DSI, do we really need to pay $5 per tonne?”

The union calculates the fee would be about US$5 (S$6.45) at current crude prices of about US$1,000 a tonne, potentially reducing the price of fresh fruit bunches by about 0.7% at a time of pressure from declining yields due to an El Nino-induced drought.

The news of the fee rate, which will be collected starting Jan 1, drove up Malaysian palm oil prices on Nov 26, as market participants expected some buyers to shift to the neighbouring country.

Indonesia and Malaysia are the two largest producers of the edible oil.

Company set up to verify export deals

Indonesia set up DSI under sovereign wealth fund Danantara to verify export transactions of palm oil, coal and ferroalloys to boost state oversight and allay concerns about transfer pricing practices and under-invoicing.

DSI plans to launch a digital platform in December, requiring exporters to upload export contracts and declarations, to track and analyse goods and payments flows and check if their prices are in line with market prices and flag any price anomalies.

GAPKI is calculating the potential impact of the additional fees on palm oil farmers and companies, Yustinus said, adding that a commodity exchange planned for 2027 would also incur expenses.

The 0.5% fee would have limited impact on costs, as it is small compared to export taxes and levies exporters already pay, said Cheang Kang Wei, analyst at Singapore-based brokerage StoneX.

However, traders are concerned about how the new verification measures will affect the flow of goods.

“That adds paperwork, timing risk and a financing cost for exporters,” added Cheang. “If it slows down contracting or shipments early next year, buyers like India could lean more on Malaysian supply.” REUTERS

data.title: Malaysia wants priority over other lenders if it backs AirAsia
data.description:
KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia will require AirAsia to give it priority over other lenders if the government agrees to provide support to the budget airline, the country’s finance minister said on Nov 26.

Officials have said they are assessing ways to provide support without risking public funds. Authorities are monitoring AirAsia’s financial health as airlines around the world grapple with a jump in jet fuel prices linked to the Iran war.

AirAsia has said it was aiming to raise up to US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) from international debt markets as well as RM700 million (S$220.19 million) in local credit facilities, with the fundraising expected to be completed between December and February.

Shares in the airline, which controls about 60% of Malaysia’s domestic aviation market and employs about 26,000 people, have lost about 72% of their value in 2026.

AirAsia posted a narrower loss in the third quarter, but warned of rising fuel costs as it works to boost liquidity.

Malaysia’s Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan told Parliament that there has so far been no agreement or commitment to provide support to AirAsia, either in the form of loans, guarantees or public fund injections.

But if required, the government would look to safeguard public funds and ensure no disruptions to connectivity, he added.

“We want to ensure that public funds get the priority they deserve because we would be the saviours if we were to intervene,” Amir Hamzah said.

The government would also look to strengthen oversight of AirAsia’s board and management, Amir Hamzah said, citing a similar approach taken to assist debt-laden oil and gas services firm Vantris Energy.

“The government’s priority is the interests of the nation and the people, not the interests of shareholders,” he added.

The government’s monitoring was focused only on AirAsia’s domestic operations and not on its overseas arms or related businesses under its affiliate Capital A.

Malaysia in 2025 approved an RM1.1 billion capital injection into Vantris through redeemable convertible loan stock, a move officials have described as a strategic ecosystem rescue rather than a bailout.

The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the Covid-19 pandemic as the conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines’ costs rocketing.

Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic suspended flights on Nov 26 and intends to file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure a short-term financing solution urgently. REUTERS

data.title: Viettel-Singtel consortium breaks ground on sub-marine cable connecting Vietnam, Thailand, Singapore
data.description:
SINGAPORE – A consortium co-chaired by Vietnam’s Viettel Group and Singapore’s Singtel has begun construction of a sub-marine fibre-optic cable system connecting Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore. The cable system offers the highest bandwidth among all sub-marine cable routes connecting Vietnam to Singapore.

This marks the first international sub-marine cable project initiated and led by a Vietnamese enterprise, said Viettel in a statement on Nov 26. The project by the consortium, VTS, is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2030.

An event to mark the signing of commercial and construction contracts with Japan’s NEC Corporation and Singapore cable system company Asean Cableship was held in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, on Nov 26. Both companies are the contractors for the project.

The entire cable system will span 2,500km with a design capacity of 600 terabits per second (Tbps). The segment between Singapore and Vietnam will cover about 1,200km and offer a capacity of 240 Tbps, or roughly 2½ times the total capacity of all international cable systems currently in use by Vietnam.

By following a direct route, VTS will be the shortest sub-marine fibre-optic cable link between Vietnam and Singapore.

Once the cable is up, the round-trip data transmission time, or latency, between the two countries is expected to be 12 milliseconds, approximately 50% lower than the current average for existing routes.

This low latency will enable smoother performance for applications such as financial transactions and artificial intelligence.

The project builds on a memorandum of understanding signed between Viettel and Singtel in April 2024 to develop a direct sub-marine cable connection between Vietnam and Singapore.

Viettel, which is run by the country’s military, said that it directly led the route planning and design of the cable. These included deciding the landing points, system configuration, and overall performance.

The cable gives Vietnam an additional international connection route. This helps to reduce the country’s reliance on existing routes. Should one route encounter an issue, traffic can be rerouted to another, ensuring that internet, banking and business services face minimal disruption, said Viettel in its statement.

Lieutenant-General Tao Duc Thang, chairman and general director of Viettel, said that Viettel proactively initiated the cable system project as it does not want the development of Vietnam’s digital economy to remain overly dependent on factors beyond its control.

“Constructing a subsea fibre-optic cable system takes many years; we cannot wait until we face a capacity shortage to begin investing,” he said.

In a separate statement, Singtel said that by strengthening connectivity between Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore, the upcoming cable system will support businesses’ growing cross-border requirements and create greater opportunities for digital investment and innovation across South-east Asia.

Ng Tian Chong, CEO of Singtel Singapore, said: “The additional connectivity and network resilience it provides will also complement Asean’s ambitions under the Digital Economy Framework Agreement to deepen regional digital integration and facilitate cross-border data flows.” THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Malaysia to seek 19% tariff ceiling in US talks until Q1 2027
data.description:
KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia will continue negotiations with the United States until the first quarter 2027 to ensure overall tariffs on Malaysian goods do not exceed 19%, particularly in addressing concerns over structural excess capacity and production under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani.

He said Malaysia would continue engaging with the US Trade Representative (USTR) to present its case and prevent any additional tariff measures from pushing the overall tariff rate on Malaysian goods above the 19% level agreed under the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART).

“The US had indicated a tariff range of between 18% and 25% for Malaysia... this is the range. But we still have until the first quarter to negotiate, explain and put forward our justification why we cannot be placed in this range. Overall you also need to take into consideration that it cannot be more than 19%,” he told reporters after the official commemoration of BYD Local Assembly Plant in Malaysia.

Earlier, the media reported that the US has proposed additional tariffs of up to 18% on Malaysian goods after determining that Malaysia’s industrial policies and manufacturing practices contribute to structural excess capacity and production that Washington says burden or restrict US commerce.

Malaysia is among 14 economies facing proposed tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, with headline rates ranging from 15% to 35%. The other economies include China, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, and the European Union.

Johari said Malaysia had made its position clear to the USTR’s deputy representative, stressing that the country should retain the benefit of being among the first to sign the trade agreement.

“Look, we were the first to sign the ART, and you promised us a 19% tariff rate. We must therefore be able to enjoy that benefit. Whatever additional measures you intend to impose, including the 10% tariff related to forced labour, the total must not exceed 19%,” he said.

He highlighted that the US is looking into four areas under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, namely excess capacity, forced labour, environmental issues and state subsidies.

He said the US has finalised a 10% tariff on forced labour while measures relating to excess capacity remain under consideration.

“On excess capacity, the US has yet to finalise its position and is still working on how to implement it. However, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) has consistently maintained that Malaysia does not have excess capacity,” he said.

Johari stressed that Malaysia’s position remained unchanged despite the indicative tariff range of 18% to 25% communicated by the US under its excess capacity assessment.

Meanwhile, he said the iron and steel sectors could come under scrutiny in the excess capacity investigation, particularly over concerns that production capacity could be used to channel exports through Malaysia.

However, the semiconductor sector was excluded from the assessment at this stage, he added. BERNAMA

data.title: Black Friday? No thanks, some brands say
data.description:
LONDON/MILAN/LOS ANGELES – While most brands are dangling deep Black Friday discounts to entice shoppers, some are opting out. These holdouts want to protect profits, make a point about sustainability, or simply stand out and try to connect with a growing number of consumers wary of permanent promotions.

In Italy, fashion brand Pinko is for the first time sitting out Black Friday in 2026, with chairman Pietro Negra saying discounting can become a vicious cycle.

“By not taking part in Black Friday, we’re trying to cut off one small head of a dragon that has another thousand,” said Negra, pointing to “family & friends” promotions, private sales and other events that encourage discounting.

“That’s not the kind of relationship we want with customers, nor are those the conditions that will secure the future of the sector.”

Retailers around the world have had a challenging year with the Iran war reigniting inflation and cash-strapped consumers needing sizeable discounts to be swayed into buying.

But while giants like Amazon can afford to slash prices as they hoover up most Black Friday traffic, for small brands the discount frenzy can be a double-edged sword, impacting profitability and making shoppers less willing to pay full-price the rest of the time.

Negra said not participating in Black Friday will cost Pinko around €2 million (S$2.83 million) in revenue, but the hit to profitability is proportionally much smaller, and margin is what he is focused on.

Fighting discount fatigue

After five years of persistently high inflation, shoppers are increasingly sceptical of retailers’ pricing strategies and less likely to believe that advertised discounts reflect real savings, said Shikha Jain, a partner at Simon-Kucher consultancy in Boston.

Choosing not to embrace Black Friday is risky as competition for every dollar is fierce. But choosing to opt out may give brands a different kind of visibility and help them build trust, especially among less price-sensitive shoppers.

“There has been a serious erosion of trust,” said Jain, adding that she sees “increasing pullback, and major fatigue against inflation and the challenging environment that many Americans find themselves in.”

Brands that opt out are also angling for a slice of consumers’ attention even if it doesn’t translate into sales instantly, instilling a message or winning brownie points.

British outerwear brand Buffalo Systems says it does not participate in Black Friday because it’s a small business manufacturing in the UK, while American outdoor retailer REI closes its stores on Black Friday and gives employees a day off to spend outside instead.

The Ordinary, a skincare brand owned by beauty giant Estee Lauder, also shuts its stores for the day and runs blood donation drives in New York and Toronto instead.

Amy Bi, senior vice president of global brand at The Ordinary, said impulse-buying around Black Friday often leads to people buying products they don’t need or that aren’t right for their skin, and halting sales for the day is a way of encouraging consumers to “slow down.”

Anti-Black Friday marketing

Smaller brands may be less able to sacrifice the much-needed sales boost Black Friday provides, and are instead leaning into a contrarian kind of marketing to set themselves apart.

UpCircle, a British beauty brand that uses coffee grounds, oat husks and other food industry byproducts to make its creams and scrubs, runs its own Black Friday discounts while promoting its anti-waste ethos in Instagram posts that criticise overproduction and overconsumption, using social media slang like “landfill maxxing.”

Black Friday was popularised in the US but has gone global since the early 2000s, driven partly by Amazon and other multinational retailers.

Black Friday is “the antithesis of everything we stand for when it comes to the associations with waste, with mass consumption,” said UpCircle founder Anna Brightman.

But its anti-consumerist posts attract eyeballs in a highly competitive market, Brightman said, and the 25% discount across the range helps convince new customers to try their first product. In just three weeks around Black Friday, Upcircle makes 20% of its online sales for the year. REUTERS

data.title: Asian stocks stabilise after tech rout
data.description:
HONG KONG – Asian stocks stabilised on Nov 26 from another hard day of selling as the tech sector enjoyed a much-needed bounce, while investors took in their stride a fresh round of proposed US tariffs.

The gains came after a dip-buying afternoon rally helped US markets finish well off their initial lows as Wall Street headed into the Thanksgiving holiday on an only slightly negative note.

Beaten-down Asian tech firms led the gains on Nov 26, with Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei again at the centre of the action, having seen wild swings this week amid concerns about the AI boom, while the euphoria over Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has worn off.

Japanese chipmaker Kioxia was the standout, surging by double figures, while South Korean titan SK Hynix were also comfortably up.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225, the Kospi in Seoul and the Taipei Taiex all advanced – even if they ended off their earlier highs – while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed more than 1%. There were also gains in Sydney, Mumbai, Singapore and Jakarta. Shanghai was flat, while Bangkok, Wellington and Manila dipped.

London, Frankfurt and Paris opened sharply higher.

Global markets have whipsawed this week, with news of Huang’s return – despite an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – lighting up Asian screens on Nov 24 before a crushing drop on Nov 25.

After a stellar start to 2026, selling in the past five months has been fanned by fears over vast capital expenditure and when that will pay off, as well as rising interest rate expectations and talk of tighter AI regulation under a new Democrat-led Congress.

Some observers have said there were signs the pain could be nearing its end.

But Michael Boutros at Forex.com warned that “buyers still need to demonstrate that renewed demand extends beyond short-lived relief rallies”.

“The focus heading into December is on whether semiconductor shares can regain traction and support a broader recovery or whether the recent deterioration signals further downside.”

And analysts at Manulife said in a note: “The market rebound is encouraging, but it should not be interpreted as confirmation that the period of volatility has ended.

“Following a sharp sell-off and increasingly oversold market conditions, further near-term gains are possible. Nevertheless, investors should be prepared for additional swings.”

Expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December were given a fresh boost on Nov 25 by data showing US inflation in October at a three-year high, while economic growth for the third quarter was revised upwards.

There was little movement in reaction to the unveiling of proposed US tariffs on 14 economies following a months-long probe into alleged excess production.
